chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
The mortgage is the largest debt most households carry. Understanding fixed vs. variable rates, the term, and the amortization helps you choose a loan suited to your risk tolerance and your situation.

This guide clarifies these concepts and the questions to ask before you sign.

2026 editorial note: rates change constantly; confirm with a mortgage broker. Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

chapters.title: Fixed Rate vs. Variable Rate
chapters.html:
Understanding the main trade-off.

A fixed rate stays the same for the entire term: predictable payments and peace of mind, but often a slightly higher starting rate. A variable rate follows market fluctuations: it can cost less if rates fall or stay low, but it exposes you to rising payments or interest.

  • Fixed: predictability and security.
  • Variable: potential savings, but risk and uncertainty.
  • The right choice depends on your risk tolerance and your budget.
Émilie's tip

Choose based on your ability to sleep soundly. If a rise in your payments would leave you gasping for air, the fixed rate is often worth its small security premium.

chapters.title: Term and Amortization
chapters.html:
Telling apart two often-confused concepts.

Amortization is the total time to repay the loan (often 25 years). The term is the length of the current contract (often 5 years), at the end of which you renew under new conditions. A longer amortization lowers the monthly payment but increases the total interest paid.

At the end of each term, you renegotiate: it's a key moment to shop around again.

Émilie's tip

Don't confuse term and amortization. A shorter amortization costs less in interest over the long run; at each term renewal, shop your rate around again.

chapters.title: The Clauses That Matter
chapters.html:
Looking beyond the rate.

  • Prepayment penalties: they can be steep if your circumstances change.
  • Accelerated repayment options (extra payments) to pay it off faster.
  • Portability (transferring the loan to another property).
  • Open vs. closed mortgage.

The lowest rate isn't always the best loan: the conditions can cost you dearly at the wrong moment.

Émilie's tip

Read the penalty clauses before you sign. A loan that's slightly more expensive but flexible can save you thousands of dollars if you have to sell or refinance sooner than expected.

chapters.title: Action Plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Assess my risk tolerance (fixed vs. variable).
  2. Meet with a mortgage broker.

Within 30 days

  1. Compare rates AND conditions (penalties, portability).
  2. Choose a suitable amortization and term.

After that

  1. Shop around at each term renewal.

chapters.title: Resources & Glossary
chapters.html:
• Fixed rate: unchanged during the term, predictable.
  • Variable rate: follows the market, with potential savings and risk.
  • Amortization: total repayment period (often 25 years).
  • Term: length of the current contract (often 5 years).
  • Prepayment penalty: cost to repay or break the loan before the term ends.
